attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post. The parenthetical cites the Sparks authors but the claim is his.

semantics.note: Faithful. Says hallucinations, reliability and complex planning remained unsolved for GPT-4 as of March 2023.

contract.note: Reading 'not solved' as material failures persisting, not as denying any improvement, is the ordinary reading.

evidence.note: OpenAI launch page (14 Mar 2023) admits hallucinations remained a known limitation. This is a company disclosure, but an admission against its own interest.
The Sparks preprint (22 Mar 2023) shows GPT-4 giving an invalid Tower of Hanoi plan, and the authors describe a 'lack of ability to plan ahead'. It concerns the early model.

reviews.rationale: Sources from the time, including OpenAI's own launch page and the Sparks authors, record persistent hallucinations and planning failures. Nothing in the packet shows these were overcome. The claim holds for March 2023.

attribution.note: Marcus's own claim. The quoted paper text is the object of his claim, not the claim itself.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'because no training-data access' link and the 'serious scrutiny' standard. The claim is firm, not hedged.

contract.note: Reading it as a necessity claim is fair. But 'serious scrutiny' has no standard, and the result turns on whether contamination-robust behavioural tests count as testing the overall intelligence claim.

evidence.note: July 2023 counterfactual-task study of gpt-4-0314, done without training data. It shows component reasoning can be probed, but it tests the released checkpoint, not the early model, and does not judge the overall intelligence claim.

reviews.rationale: No evidence shows training-data access is indispensable. The only counterevidence, e6, tests a different checkpoint and only component capabilities. The packet itself notes these gaps. The evidence settles neither the necessity claim nor its refutation.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: Keeps the absolute 'absolutely nothing', with architecture and training set as examples.

contract.note: The contract allows for hyperbole and separates model family from full details. Whether a one-line note (Transformer-style, next-token, RLHF, public plus licensed data) counts as substantive decides the result.

evidence.note: The 16 Mar 2023 report discloses a Transformer-style architecture, next-token pretraining, RLHF, and broad data sources. That contradicts the literal absolute. The same section says it withholds model size, dataset construction and other details.

reviews.rationale: The literal 'absolutely nothing' is false: OpenAI disclosed the model family, training objective, use of RLHF and broad data sources. The substantive part holds. No architectural details such as size were given, and the training set was described only in the vaguest terms, as the report itself says.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: Faithful. The comparison baseline ('before') is left unspecified, as in the source.

contract.note: Reading it as continuity in kind, allowing gains in degree, is fair. With no boundary between qualitative and quantitative change, the result depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: The technical report shows GPT-4 beats GPT-3.5 on most exams. These are gains in degree and do not settle whether its capabilities differ in kind.
OpenAI's launch post says GPT-4 has limitations similar to earlier GPT models. That supports the weaknesses half only, and it is a company disclosure.

reviews.rationale: Continuity of weaknesses has support, though only from OpenAI's own disclosure. Whether the strengths are qualitatively the same is not settled: e1 shows only score gains, and no taxonomy separates change in kind from change in degree. The support condition requires both halves, and nothing establishes a contradiction.
